basics.label: Comprehension
basics.value: [f(x) for x in rows if keep(x)]

patterns.title: Index once, look up many
patterns.why: Replace repeated scans with one dictionary index.
patterns.remember: A dictionary is the standard repeated key-lookup pattern.

patterns.title: Stream with a generator
patterns.why: Process streams incrementally instead of materializing everything.
patterns.remember: Use yield for files, API pages and large record streams.

patterns.title: Own resource lifetime with a context manager
patterns.code:
from pathlib import Path

with Path("events.jsonl").open() as handle:
    for line in handle:
        process(line)
patterns.why: Context managers make cleanup deterministic even when an exception occurs.
patterns.remember: If something must be closed/released, prefer a with block around its lifetime.

patterns.title: Catch expected exceptions at the boundary
patterns.why: Narrow exception handling adds useful domain context without hiding unrelated failures.
patterns.remember: Catch what you expect, add context, preserve the original cause.

patterns.title: Use a dataclass for a small explicit record
patterns.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Event:
    id: str
    occurred_at: datetime
    amount: float
patterns.why: A dataclass gives named typed fields and generated value-oriented behavior without manual boilerplate.
patterns.remember: Use it when a tuple/dict has become a real domain record with stable fields.

apis.name: enumerate
apis.example: for i, row in enumerate(rows, start=1): ...

apis.name: zip
apis.example: for name, score in zip(names, scores): ...

apis.name: contextlib.contextmanager
apis.whatFor: Build a context manager around setup/cleanup.

practices.title: Deduplicate in order
practices.prompt: Keep the first occurrence of each event_id.
practices.reveal: Maintain a set for membership and append only unseen IDs.

practices.title: Stream a huge file
practices.prompt: Process millions of records without loading all rows into memory.
practices.reveal: Yield or iterate records incrementally instead of returning one giant list.

patterns.title: Readable method chain
patterns.code:
result = (
    orders
    .query("status == 'paid'")
    .assign(revenue=lambda d: d["qty"] * d["price"])
    .groupby("country", as_index=False)
    .agg(revenue=("revenue", "sum"))
)
patterns.why: Keep a transformation visible top to bottom.
patterns.remember: Method chains work best when each step changes the same DataFrame conceptually.

patterns.title: Validate joins
patterns.code:
enriched = orders.merge(
    customers,
    on="customer_id",
    how="left",
    validate="m:1",
    indicator=True,
)
patterns.why: Join cardinality bugs can silently multiply rows.
patterns.remember: validate and indicator make assumptions explicit.

patterns.title: Latest row per business key
patterns.code:
latest = (
    events
    .sort_values(["customer_id", "updated_at"])
    .drop_duplicates("customer_id", keep="last")
)
patterns.why: Sort explicitly, then keep one deterministic winner per key.
patterns.remember: In Pandas, latest-row logic is usually sort_values + drop_duplicates.

patterns.title: Keep rows missing from the other table
patterns.code:
missing = (
    source.merge(target[["id"]], on="id", how="left", indicator=True)
    .loc[lambda d: d["_merge"].eq("left_only")]
    .drop(columns="_merge")
)
patterns.why: A left merge with an indicator makes unmatched rows explicit and debuggable.
patterns.remember: Pandas anti-join = left merge + indicator + left_only.

patterns.title: Named grouped aggregation
patterns.code:
summary = (
    orders.groupby("customer_id", as_index=False)
    .agg(
        order_count=("order_id", "size"),
        revenue=("amount", "sum"),
    )
)
patterns.why: Named aggregation keeps output column names close to their source and aggregation function.
patterns.remember: Pandas grain = groupby keys; use named agg for readable outputs.

apis.name: assign
apis.whatFor: Add derived columns in a chain.

apis.name: DataFrame.merge
apis.whatFor: Join DataFrames with optional cardinality validation.

practices.title: Latest order per customer
practices.prompt: Keep one newest order per customer.
practices.reveal: Sort by timestamp descending, then drop_duplicates on customer_id.

practices.title: Join without row explosion
practices.prompt: Orders are many-to-one with customers and row count must stay stable.
practices.reveal: Declare expected cardinality and inspect unmatched rows.

patterns.title: Expression pipeline
patterns.code:
result = (
    df
    .filter(pl.col("status") == "paid")
    .with_columns((pl.col("qty") * pl.col("price")).alias("revenue"))
    .group_by("country")
    .agg(pl.col("revenue").sum())
)
patterns.why: Expressions give Polars room to optimize and parallelize.
patterns.remember: Think column expressions, not row-wise Python.

patterns.title: Lazy scan
patterns.code:
result = (
    pl.scan_parquet("events/*.parquet")
    .filter(pl.col("event_date") >= cutoff)
    .select(["user_id", "amount"])
    .group_by("user_id")
    .agg(pl.col("amount").sum())
    .collect()
)
patterns.why: Lazy scans can push filters and projections down.
patterns.remember: Use scan_* for analytical file pipelines and collect at the boundary.

patterns.title: Latest row per business key
patterns.code:
latest = (
    df
    .sort(["customer_id", "updated_at"])
    .unique(subset=["customer_id"], keep="last")
)
patterns.why: Ordered unique selection expresses a compact top-one-per-key pattern.
patterns.remember: Sort by the tie-breaker first, then unique on the business key.

patterns.title: Anti-join directly
patterns.code:
missing = source.join(
    target.select("id"),
    on="id",
    how="anti",
)
patterns.why: Polars exposes anti join as a first-class join strategy.
patterns.remember: Use how='anti' when you only need left rows with no match.

patterns.title: Expression grouped aggregation
patterns.code:
summary = (
    orders.group_by("customer_id")
    .agg(
        pl.len().alias("order_count"),
        pl.col("amount").sum().alias("revenue"),
    )
)
patterns.why: Polars keeps aggregation logic as optimized expressions.
patterns.remember: Polars grain = group_by keys; every agg expression returns one value per group.

apis.name: with_columns
apis.whatFor: Add or replace columns through expressions.

practices.title: Latest row per user
practices.prompt: Read large Parquet and keep latest event.
practices.reveal: Scan lazily, filter early, sort by event time, then keep one row per user.

practices.title: Large Parquet transform
practices.prompt: Filter and aggregate many files with minimal I/O.
practices.reveal: Use a LazyFrame, filter/select early, collect at the boundary.

technologies.name: Spark / PySpark
technologies.tagline: Partitions, shuffles, joins and DataFrame execution.

basics.label: Rule
basics.value: Watch shuffle, skew and tiny files

patterns.title: Latest row per key
patterns.code:
w = Window.partitionBy("customer_id").orderBy(F.col("updated_at").desc())

latest = (
    df
    .withColumn("_rn", F.row_number().over(w))
    .filter(F.col("_rn") == 1)
    .drop("_rn")
)
patterns.why: Window functions express ordered per-key logic without collecting.
patterns.remember: row_number is the standard deterministic dedupe shape.

patterns.title: Broadcast small dimension
patterns.code:
result = fact.join(
    F.broadcast(dim),
    on="country_id",
    how="left"
)
patterns.why: Broadcast can avoid shuffling a large fact relation.
patterns.remember: Broadcast only genuinely small data and confirm the plan.

patterns.title: Read the physical plan before tuning
patterns.code:
query = (
    fact.join(dim, 'country_id')
    .groupBy('country_id')
    .agg(F.sum('amount').alias('revenue'))
)

query.explain("formatted")
patterns.why: The physical plan reveals exchanges, join strategies and scans that explain where distributed work happens.
patterns.remember: Tune what Spark actually planned, not what you assume the code means.

patterns.title: Choose repartition vs coalesce deliberately
patterns.code:
# redistribute by a useful key
balanced = df.repartition("customer_id")

# reduce output partitions after filtering
smaller = filtered.coalesce(16)
patterns.why: repartition performs a shuffle to rebalance/change partitioning; coalesce is commonly used to reduce partitions with less movement.
patterns.remember: Repartition to redistribute; coalesce mainly to shrink partition count.

patterns.title: Cache only reused expensive intermediates
patterns.code:
base = expensive_transform(events).cache()

daily = base.groupBy("event_date").count()
by_type = base.groupBy("event_type").count()

base.unpersist()
patterns.why: Caching can avoid recomputation when the same expensive lineage is reused, but consumes cluster memory/storage.
patterns.remember: Cache for reuse, not by habit; unpersist when the reuse window is over.

practices.title: Skewed aggregation
practices.prompt: One key owns 40% of rows.
practices.reveal: Confirm skew first, then consider salting or a different aggregation plan.

practices.title: Repeated expensive branch
practices.prompt: Two downstream reports reuse the same costly cleaned DataFrame.
practices.reveal: Cache the reused intermediate, trigger reuse, then unpersist.

technologies.name: PySpark
technologies.tagline: Spark DataFrame patterns expressed through Python APIs.

basics.label: Rule
basics.value: Prefer Spark built-ins over Python UDFs

patterns.title: Latest row per business key
patterns.code:
w = Window.partitionBy("customer_id").orderBy(
    F.col("updated_at").desc()
)

latest = (
    df
    .withColumn("_rn", F.row_number().over(w))
    .filter(F.col("_rn") == 1)
    .drop("_rn")
)
patterns.why: Window functions express ordered per-key logic without collecting data to the driver.
patterns.remember: Use row_number for deterministic deduplication when you have a clear ordering column.

patterns.title: Prefer built-in Spark expressions
patterns.code:
clean = df.withColumn(
    "email_domain",
    F.lower(F.element_at(F.split(F.col("email"), "@"), -1))
)
patterns.why: Built-in expressions stay inside Spark's optimized execution engine.
patterns.remember: Check pyspark.sql.functions before reaching for a Python UDF.

patterns.title: Left anti join
patterns.code:
missing = source.join(
    target.select("id"),
    on="id",
    how="left_anti",
)
patterns.why: Spark's left_anti join avoids carrying right-side columns when you only need non-matches.
patterns.remember: PySpark anti-join = how='left_anti'.

patterns.title: Distributed grouped aggregation
patterns.code:
summary = (
    orders.groupBy("customer_id")
    .agg(
        F.count("*").alias("order_count"),
        F.sum("amount").alias("revenue"),
    )
)
patterns.why: groupBy changes the physical data distribution and usually introduces a shuffle.
patterns.remember: In Spark, GROUP BY is a wide operation: reason about grain and shuffle together.

apis.name: pyspark.sql.functions
apis.signature: from pyspark.sql import functions as F
apis.whatFor: Use Spark SQL expressions from Python.

apis.name: DataFrame.join
apis.whatFor: Join Spark DataFrames using explicit join semantics.

practices.title: Incremental CDC dedupe
practices.prompt: Keep only the newest record per primary key.
practices.reveal: Partition by the business key, order by sequence/timestamp descending, then keep row_number = 1.

practices.title: Find missing target keys
practices.prompt: Keep source rows whose IDs do not exist in target.
practices.reveal: Use a left anti join rather than joining and filtering null right columns.

technologies.name: Apache Airflow
technologies.tagline: DAG design, retries, schedules and task boundaries.

patterns.title: TaskFlow DAG
patterns.why: TaskFlow keeps dependency wiring close to Python.
patterns.remember: Tasks should be meaningful retryable operational boundaries.

patterns.title: Dynamic task mapping
patterns.why: Dynamic task mapping creates separate runtime task instances from upstream data, preserving retries and observability per mapped item.
patterns.remember: Use expand() when the number of parallel task instances is known only at run time.

patterns.title: Idempotent partition from the data interval
patterns.why: Airflow schedules logical data intervals; using that interval makes backfills and retries target the same business slice.
patterns.remember: A retry should rewrite the same logical partition, not append a second copy.

patterns.title: Pass metadata, not datasets
patterns.why: TaskFlow can move small results through XCom, but large datasets belong in durable storage.
patterns.remember: XCom should coordinate tasks; object storage/database tables should carry the data.

apis.name: expand
apis.whatFor: Create mapped task instances at runtime.

practices.title: Backfillable daily ingestion
practices.prompt: Rerun one day safely.
practices.reveal: Parameterize writes by the logical interval and make them idempotent.

practices.title: Runtime list of partitions
practices.prompt: An upstream discovery task returns a variable list of dates to process.
practices.reveal: Return the dates, then expand the processing task over them.

technologies.name: dbt
technologies.tagline: SQL models, ref/source, incremental logic and tests.

patterns.title: Thin staging model
patterns.code:
select
  cast(order_id as bigint) as order_id,
  cast(order_ts as timestamp) as order_ts,
  amount
from {{ source('raw', 'orders') }}
patterns.why: Normalize names and types close to the source.
patterns.remember: Keep staging mechanical; move business meaning downstream.

patterns.title: Incremental lookback
patterns.why: Process changes while tolerating late arrivals.
patterns.remember: Incremental logic must remain correct on a full refresh.

patterns.title: Put grain assumptions into tests
patterns.code:
models:
  - name: dim_customer
    columns:
      - name: customer_id
        data_tests:
          - not_null
          - unique
      - name: country_code
        data_tests:
          - relationships:
              arguments:
                to: ref('dim_country')
                field: country_code
patterns.why: Tests turn model-grain and relationship expectations into executable project contracts.
patterns.remember: Test the key, nullability, accepted domain, and important relationships—not every column indiscriminately.

patterns.title: Extract repeated SQL into a macro
patterns.why: Macros remove repeated SQL syntax while keeping the model dependency graph in ordinary ref/source calls.
patterns.remember: Use macros for repeated transformation mechanics, not to hide the entire model behind metaprogramming.

patterns.title: Declare source expectations
patterns.code:
sources:
  - name: raw
    schema: landing
    tables:
      - name: orders
        loaded_at_field: ingested_at
        freshness:
          warn_after: {count: 2, period: hour}
          error_after: {count: 6, period: hour}
patterns.why: Source metadata makes upstream data availability an explicit part of the analytics contract.
patterns.remember: A transformation can be logically correct and still be wrong for users if the source is stale.

apis.name: is_incremental
apis.whatFor: Branch SQL logic only during incremental execution.

practices.title: Late-arriving facts
practices.prompt: Source can revise 48 hours.
practices.reveal: Use a safety window and merge on a stable unique key.

practices.title: Repeated currency conversion
practices.prompt: Many models repeat the same cents-to-decimal SQL.
practices.reveal: Extract the mechanical SQL expression into a small reusable macro.

technologies.name: SQL
technologies.tagline: Portable joins, windows, CTEs and aggregation.

basics.label: CTE
basics.value: with base as (...) select ... from base

basics.label: Conditional agg
basics.value: sum(case when ... then amount else 0 end)

patterns.title: Latest row per key
patterns.why: Ranking windows solve deterministic top-N per group.
patterns.remember: Partition defines the group; order defines the winner.

patterns.title: Anti-join
patterns.code:
select s.*
from source_rows s
left join target_rows t
  on t.id = s.id
where t.id is null;
patterns.why: Find rows present on one side and absent on the other.
patterns.remember: NOT EXISTS is an equally useful anti-join shape.

patterns.title: Grouped aggregation
patterns.code:
select
  customer_id,
  count(*) as order_count,
  sum(amount) as revenue
from orders
group by customer_id;
patterns.why: Aggregate at the required business grain and name each derived measure explicitly.
patterns.remember: The GROUP BY columns define the output grain.

patterns.title: Compare each row to the previous event
patterns.code:
select
  user_id,
  event_ts,
  lag(event_ts) over (
    partition by user_id
    order by event_ts
  ) as previous_event_ts
from events;
patterns.why: LAG reads a previous row within an ordered partition without a self-join.
patterns.remember: Partition defines whose history you compare; order defines what 'previous' means.

patterns.title: Turn row conditions into measures
patterns.code:
select
  customer_id,
  sum(case when status = 'paid' then amount else 0 end) as paid_revenue,
  sum(case when status = 'refund' then amount else 0 end) as refunded
from orders
group by customer_id;
patterns.why: Conditional aggregation computes multiple business measures at one grouped grain.
patterns.remember: Keep the GROUP BY grain fixed; change the CASE expression for each metric.

apis.name: ROW_NUMBER
apis.example: row_number() over (partition by id order by ts desc)

apis.name: LAG
apis.example: lag(status) over (partition by id order by ts)

practices.title: Consecutive activity
practices.prompt: Find gaps between user events.
practices.reveal: Use LAG(event_ts) partitioned by user and compare timestamps.

practices.title: Paid vs refunded revenue
practices.prompt: Create several measures at the same customer grain.
practices.reveal: Group once and use CASE inside SUM for each measure.

patterns.title: Query files directly
patterns.why: Query columnar files without loading them into a server database.
patterns.remember: Push filters and projections into the scan.

patterns.title: Anti-join with NOT EXISTS
patterns.code:
select s.*
from source_rows s
where not exists (
  select 1
  from target_rows t
  where t.id = s.id
);
patterns.why: NOT EXISTS is a clear null-safe anti-join idiom in SQL engines including DuckDB.
patterns.remember: Use NOT EXISTS when the question is 'which left rows have no right match?'.

patterns.title: Aggregate files at business grain
patterns.why: DuckDB can aggregate directly over files without a separate ingestion step.
patterns.remember: Push projection/filtering into the file scan, then aggregate at the required grain.

patterns.title: Materialize a reusable Parquet result
patterns.why: COPY turns an analytical query result into an efficient reusable columnar artifact.
patterns.remember: Query raw flexibly; materialize clean reusable outputs as Parquet.

patterns.title: Inspect query execution before rewriting SQL
patterns.why: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows the executed operator tree and timing information.
patterns.remember: Measure scans, joins and aggregates before changing a query blindly.

practices.title: Local lake query
practices.prompt: Aggregate partitioned Parquet without ingestion.
practices.reveal: Query the glob directly and filter before aggregation.

practices.title: CSV repeatedly queried
practices.prompt: A cleaned CSV query will be reused many times.
practices.reveal: Materialize the cleaned query result as compressed Parquet.

technologies.name: Delta Lake
technologies.tagline: Transactional lakehouse merge and history patterns.

basics.label: MERGE
basics.value: merge into target using source on ...

patterns.title: Idempotent upsert
patterns.code:
merge into silver.customers as t
using updates as s
on t.customer_id = s.customer_id
when matched and s.updated_at > t.updated_at then
  update set *
when not matched then
  insert *;
patterns.why: MERGE applies insert/update logic atomically.
patterns.remember: Stable keys and ordering guards matter for CDC.

patterns.title: Use table history for reproducible debugging
patterns.why: Transaction history and time travel let you inspect or reproduce a prior table state.
patterns.remember: When a table changed unexpectedly, identify the commit first, then compare versions.

patterns.title: Treat schema evolution as an explicit decision
patterns.code:
(
  updates.write
  .format("delta")
  .option("mergeSchema", "true")
  .mode("append")
  .save(path)
)
patterns.why: Delta can evolve schemas, but enabling evolution should be intentional because it changes the table contract.
patterns.remember: Schema drift is a contract change; review it instead of silently accepting every new column.

patterns.title: Replace the same logical batch on retry
patterns.code:
condition = "event_date = '2026-09-21'"
(
  batch.write
  .format("delta")
  .mode("overwrite")
  .option("replaceWhere", condition)
  .saveAsTable("silver.events")
)
patterns.why: Predicate-scoped replacement can make a deterministic batch retry rewrite only its target partition.
patterns.remember: A batch rerun should replace its logical slice rather than append duplicates.

apis.name: MERGE INTO
apis.signature: MERGE INTO target USING source ON ...

apis.name: replaceWhere
apis.whatFor: Overwrite only data matching a deterministic predicate.

practices.title: CDC upsert
practices.prompt: Ignore older late updates.
practices.reveal: Update only when the incoming sequence/timestamp is newer.

practices.title: Retry one failed daily partition
practices.prompt: Rerunning must not duplicate already written data.
practices.reveal: Replace exactly the logical date partition instead of appending.

patterns.title: Latest row with QUALIFY
patterns.why: QUALIFY filters window results without wrapping the query in another CTE.
patterns.remember: BigQuery latest-row = ROW_NUMBER + QUALIFY.

patterns.title: Upsert with MERGE
patterns.code:
merge `analytics.customers` t
using staging_customers s
on t.customer_id = s.customer_id
when matched and s.updated_at > t.updated_at then
  update set name = s.name, updated_at = s.updated_at
when not matched then
  insert (customer_id, name, updated_at)
  values (s.customer_id, s.name, s.updated_at);
patterns.why: MERGE expresses insert/update logic in one atomic warehouse statement.
patterns.remember: Match on the stable business key and guard updates with ordering when source events can arrive late.

patterns.title: Flatten repeated fields with UNNEST
patterns.code:
select
  order_id,
  item.sku,
  item.quantity
from `raw.orders`
cross join unnest(items) as item;
patterns.why: UNNEST converts array elements into rows so nested records can participate in relational operations.
patterns.remember: Every UNNEST can multiply rows; validate cardinality before aggregating.

patterns.title: Prune partitions explicitly
patterns.code:
select customer_id, sum(amount) as revenue
from `analytics.orders`
where order_date between date '2026-09-01' and date '2026-09-21'
group by customer_id;
patterns.why: Filtering on the partitioning column limits scanned partitions and usually reduces cost and latency.
patterns.remember: Partition filters are both a correctness boundary and a cost-control habit.

patterns.title: Make dirty casts non-fatal
patterns.code:
select
  safe_cast(raw_customer_id as int64) as customer_id,
  safe_cast(raw_amount as numeric) as amount
from landing.orders;
patterns.why: SAFE_CAST returns NULL rather than aborting the whole query when a value cannot be converted.
patterns.remember: Use safe casts at dirty ingestion boundaries, then measure and handle the resulting NULLs.

apis.name: QUALIFY
apis.whatFor: Filter after window functions are evaluated.

apis.name: UNNEST
apis.whatFor: Expand repeated array values into rows.

apis.name: SAFE_CAST
apis.whatFor: Return NULL rather than fail invalid casts.

practices.title: Nested order lines
practices.prompt: Orders contain an array of item structs. Compute revenue by SKU.
practices.reveal: UNNEST items first, compute line revenue, then group by SKU.

practices.title: Latest customer snapshot
practices.prompt: Keep the latest record per customer without a wrapper CTE.
practices.reveal: Use ROW_NUMBER over customer_id ordered by updated_at descending and QUALIFY = 1.

patterns.title: Latest row with QUALIFY
patterns.why: Snowflake QUALIFY applies after analytical windows and keeps the query flat.
patterns.remember: Snowflake and BigQuery share the same QUALIFY mental model.

patterns.title: Upsert with MERGE
patterns.code:
merge into analytics.customers t
using staging_customers s
on t.customer_id = s.customer_id
when matched and s.updated_at > t.updated_at then
  update set name = s.name, updated_at = s.updated_at
when not matched then
  insert (customer_id, name, updated_at)
  values (s.customer_id, s.name, s.updated_at);
patterns.why: Snowflake MERGE handles matched and unmatched rows in a single statement.
patterns.remember: Deduplicate the source before MERGE when multiple source rows can target the same key.

patterns.title: Project typed columns from VARIANT
patterns.code:
select
  payload:customer:id::string as customer_id,
  payload:amount::number(18,2) as amount
from raw_events
where payload:type::string = 'order';
patterns.why: VARIANT lets semi-structured data land quickly while typed projections create a stable downstream contract.
patterns.remember: Keep raw flexibility at landing; cast into stable types at the semantic boundary.

patterns.title: Expand nested arrays with FLATTEN
patterns.why: FLATTEN turns array/object members into rows while retaining correlation to the source row.
patterns.remember: FLATTEN changes row cardinality—check counts before and after.

patterns.title: Quarantine invalid values with TRY conversions
patterns.code:
select
  try_to_number(raw_amount, 18, 2) as amount,
  try_to_timestamp_ntz(raw_ts) as event_ts
from landing.events;
patterns.why: TRY conversion functions return NULL for invalid values instead of failing the entire statement.
patterns.remember: Use TRY_* at ingestion boundaries, then profile invalid NULL outcomes separately.

apis.name: TRY_TO_NUMBER
apis.whatFor: Convert dirty numeric text without failing the statement.

practices.title: Flatten nested items
practices.prompt: Extract one row per item from a VARIANT order payload.
practices.reveal: Flatten payload:items and cast item.value fields to stable types.

practices.title: Safe landing conversion
practices.prompt: Some numeric strings are invalid but the load should continue.
practices.reveal: Use TRY_TO_NUMBER, then measure rows where the result is NULL.

patterns.title: Latest child row with OUTER APPLY
patterns.code:
select c.customer_id, x.status, x.updated_at
from dbo.customer c
outer apply (
  select top (1) s.status, s.updated_at
  from dbo.customer_status s
  where s.customer_id = c.customer_id
  order by s.updated_at desc
) x;
patterns.why: OUTER APPLY is a useful SQL Server-specific top-one-per-parent shape.
patterns.remember: Use OUTER APPLY when you want the parent preserved even without a child row.

patterns.title: Top child per parent with OUTER APPLY
patterns.code:
select
  c.customer_id,
  x.order_id,
  x.order_date
from dbo.customer c
outer apply (
  select top (1) o.order_id, o.order_date
  from dbo.orders o
  where o.customer_id = c.customer_id
  order by o.order_date desc
) x;
patterns.why: APPLY is useful for correlated table expressions such as top-N related rows.
patterns.remember: OUTER APPLY preserves the parent even when the correlated expression returns no row.

patterns.title: Materialize a reusable intermediate into a temp table
patterns.why: A temp table can clarify multi-step procedures and can be indexed when the intermediate is reused.
patterns.remember: Materialize when reuse, statistics or debugging justify it—not for every CTE.

patterns.title: Convert dirty input without aborting the batch
patterns.code:
select
  try_convert(date, raw_order_date) as order_date,
  try_convert(decimal(18,2), raw_amount) as amount
from staging.orders;
patterns.why: TRY_CONVERT returns NULL for invalid inputs and lets the batch continue.
patterns.remember: Safe conversion is useful at staging boundaries; invalid NULLs still need quality checks.

patterns.title: Running total with an ordered window
patterns.code:
select
  customer_id,
  order_date,
  sum(amount) over (
    partition by customer_id
    order by order_date
    rows between unbounded preceding and current row
  ) as running_revenue
from dbo.orders;
patterns.why: An explicit ROWS frame makes the cumulative window semantics visible.
patterns.remember: Partition chooses the entity; order chooses sequence; frame chooses which rows contribute.

apis.name: OUTER APPLY
apis.whatFor: Run a correlated table expression while preserving left rows.

apis.name: TRY_CONVERT
apis.whatFor: Convert invalid input to NULL rather than failing.

practices.title: Latest order per customer
practices.prompt: Return every customer and their newest order, including customers with no orders.
practices.reveal: Correlate an ordered TOP (1) subquery through OUTER APPLY.

practices.title: Reusable heavy intermediate
practices.prompt: A procedure reuses the same grouped result three times.
practices.reveal: Materialize into #temp and index the join key if repeated use justifies it.

patterns.title: Latest row with DISTINCT ON
patterns.code:
select distinct on (customer_id)
  customer_id, status, updated_at
from customer_status
order by customer_id, updated_at desc;
patterns.why: PostgreSQL DISTINCT ON is a concise top-one-per-group idiom.
patterns.remember: ORDER BY must start with the DISTINCT ON key, then define the winner.

patterns.title: Upsert with ON CONFLICT
patterns.code:
insert into customers (customer_id, name, updated_at)
values ($1, $2, $3)
on conflict (customer_id) do update
set name = excluded.name,
    updated_at = excluded.updated_at
where excluded.updated_at > customers.updated_at;
patterns.why: PostgreSQL ON CONFLICT is the canonical insert-or-update shape for a unique key.
patterns.remember: The conflict target must be backed by a unique constraint/index.

patterns.title: Project fields from JSONB
patterns.code:
select
  payload ->> 'event_type' as event_type,
  payload #>> '{customer,id}' as customer_id
from raw_events;
patterns.why: JSONB operators let you extract scalar values while preserving the original semi-structured payload.
patterns.remember: Use -> for JSON, ->> for text, and #>> for a nested text path.

patterns.title: Inspect actual plan and buffer use
patterns.code:
explain (analyze, buffers)
select customer_id, sum(amount)
from orders
where order_date >= current_date - 30
group by customer_id;
patterns.why: Actual execution plus buffer statistics show whether time is spent scanning, joining, sorting or reading pages.
patterns.remember: Check the real plan before adding an index or rewriting the query.

patterns.title: Correlate a top-N subquery with LATERAL
patterns.code:
select c.customer_id, o.order_id, o.order_date
from customer c
left join lateral (
  select order_id, order_date
  from orders o
  where o.customer_id = c.customer_id
  order by order_date desc
  limit 1
) o on true;
patterns.why: LATERAL allows a subquery in FROM to reference columns from rows produced earlier in the FROM list.
patterns.remember: Use LATERAL when each parent row needs its own small correlated relation.

apis.whatFor: Inspect the actual execution plan and buffer activity.

practices.title: Idempotent event sink
practices.prompt: Load events keyed by event_id without duplicate inserts.
practices.reveal: Create a unique constraint and use DO NOTHING or DO UPDATE according to semantics.

practices.title: Slow filtered aggregation
practices.prompt: A query became slow as orders grew.
practices.reveal: Inspect the real scan/aggregate plan before proposing an index.

patterns.title: Latest row with ROW_NUMBER
patterns.why: Window ranking keeps all columns from the winning record.
patterns.remember: Use ROW_NUMBER when you need the complete latest row, not only MAX(timestamp).

patterns.title: Upsert on a unique-key collision
patterns.code:
insert into customer(customer_id, name, updated_at)
values (?, ?, ?)
on duplicate key update
  name = values(name),
  updated_at = values(updated_at);
patterns.why: A duplicate-key clause turns a unique-key conflict into an update path.
patterns.remember: The unique key defines the conflict boundary; be explicit about fields allowed to change.

patterns.title: Read typed values from JSON
patterns.code:
select
  json_unquote(json_extract(payload, '$.event_type')) as event_type,
  json_extract(payload, '$.amount') as amount
from raw_events;
patterns.why: JSON functions allow semi-structured payloads to coexist with relational columns.
patterns.remember: Extract intentionally and cast/validate values before downstream arithmetic or joins.

patterns.title: Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE before guessing
patterns.code:
explain analyze
select customer_id, sum(amount)
from orders
where order_date >= current_date - interval 30 day
group by customer_id;
patterns.why: The execution plan shows access paths and actual operator timing for the query.
patterns.remember: Observe the plan first; indexes are a response to access patterns, not a default fix.

practices.title: Latest complete status row
practices.prompt: Return every column from the newest status per customer.
practices.reveal: Rank by updated_at descending inside customer partitions and keep rn=1.

practices.title: Dirty event payload
practices.prompt: Extract JSON amount values before aggregation.
practices.reveal: Extract the path, cast/validate it, and profile malformed rows.

patterns.title: FastAPI core pattern
patterns.code: Pydantic, Depends, response models, HTTPException
patterns.why: A compact recognition card for FastAPI.
patterns.remember: Use this page as a launch point; AI refreshes can expand it into deeper version-aware patterns.

patterns.title: Inject request-scoped dependencies
patterns.why: Dependency injection keeps connection/session lifecycle out of route business logic and makes dependencies replaceable in tests.
patterns.remember: Use Depends for request-scoped infrastructure and reusable boundary checks.

patterns.title: Separate input and response contracts
patterns.why: Explicit request/response models make the public API contract clearer than leaking internal persistence objects.
patterns.remember: Validate at the HTTP boundary; return a deliberately shaped response model.

patterns.title: Defer small after-response work
patterns.why: BackgroundTasks is suitable for lightweight work that can happen after the response in the same application process.
patterns.remember: Use it for small after-response tasks; use an external worker/queue for heavy or distributed jobs.

patterns.title: Map domain errors at the HTTP boundary
patterns.why: A centralized exception handler prevents HTTP details from leaking through service/domain code.
patterns.remember: Domain code raises domain errors; the API boundary decides the HTTP status and response shape.

apis.name: BackgroundTasks
apis.whatFor: Run small same-process work after the response.

apis.name: response_model
apis.whatFor: Declare and filter the public response contract.

practices.title: Database-backed route
practices.prompt: Use a DB session without global mutable state.
practices.reveal: Inject the session with Depends and close it through the dependency lifecycle.

practices.title: Confirmation email
practices.prompt: Return an HTTP response before a small email task finishes.
practices.reveal: Schedule the small same-process task after committing the request work.

patterns.title: Kubernetes core pattern
patterns.code: Deployment, Service, probes, requests and limits
patterns.why: A compact recognition card for Kubernetes.
patterns.remember: Use this page as a launch point; AI refreshes can expand it into deeper version-aware patterns.

patterns.title: Use startup, readiness and liveness for different questions
patterns.why: Startup delays liveness/readiness until initialization succeeds; readiness controls traffic; liveness controls restarts.
patterns.remember: Ready means receive traffic. Live means restart me if false. Startup protects slow initialization.

patterns.title: Set requests before tuning limits
patterns.code:
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: "250m"
    memory: 256Mi
  limits:
    memory: 512Mi
patterns.why: Requests inform scheduling and reserved capacity; limits constrain runtime consumption.
patterns.remember: Requests answer 'what do I need to schedule?'; limits answer 'how far may I go?'.

patterns.title: Separate configuration from the image
patterns.code:
env:
  - name: LOG_LEVEL
    valueFrom:
      configMapKeyRef:
        name: api-config
        key: log_level
  - name: DATABASE_PASSWORD
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: api-secret
        key: password
patterns.why: Environment-specific configuration should not require rebuilding the container image.
patterns.remember: ConfigMap for ordinary config; Secret for sensitive values; keep both outside the image.

patterns.title: Deploy immutable versions through a Deployment
patterns.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: api }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: api }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: example/api:1.4.2
patterns.why: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets and rolls the desired pod template toward the declared version.
patterns.remember: Change the immutable image version in desired state; let the controller reconcile replicas.

apis.name: kubectl describe
apis.whatFor: Inspect desired/current state and recent events.

practices.title: Slow-starting API
practices.prompt: The application needs 45 seconds to initialize and liveness keeps restarting it.
practices.reveal: Use startupProbe to protect initialization, readiness for traffic and liveness for deadlock recovery.

practices.title: Unschedulable pods
practices.prompt: A Deployment stays Pending after a resource change.
practices.reveal: Inspect pod events and compare requests with available node capacity.

patterns.title: Linux core pattern
patterns.code: find, grep, journalctl, ss, lsof
patterns.why: A compact recognition card for Linux.
patterns.remember: Use this page as a launch point; AI refreshes can expand it into deeper version-aware patterns.

patterns.title: Trace a failing service from logs
patterns.code:
systemctl status api.service
journalctl -u api.service --since "30 minutes ago"
journalctl -u api.service -f
patterns.why: systemd status gives current unit state; journalctl gives the timeline needed to explain the failure.
patterns.remember: State tells you what; logs usually tell you why.

patterns.title: Find the process owning a port
patterns.code:
ss -ltnp
lsof -i :8000
ps -fp <pid>
patterns.why: Binding failures are usually easier to solve by identifying the listener than by repeatedly changing application settings.
patterns.remember: socket -> PID -> process -> decide whether to stop it or change the port.

patterns.title: Fail shell scripts visibly
patterns.why: Strict shell settings catch unset variables and pipeline failures that would otherwise continue silently.
patterns.remember: Quote variables, validate inputs, and make failure explicit.

apis.name: ss
apis.whatFor: Inspect listening TCP sockets and owning processes.

apis.name: find
apis.whatFor: Locate files by type/name/time or other metadata.

practices.title: Port already in use
practices.prompt: An API cannot bind to port 8000.
practices.reveal: Identify the listener, trace the PID, then decide whether to stop it or change the port.

practices.title: Service crashes after deploy
practices.prompt: A systemd service immediately exits.
practices.reveal: Check service state, then inspect the recent unit journal for the root error.

patterns.title: PowerShell core pattern
patterns.code: Where-Object, Select-Object, Invoke-RestMethod
patterns.why: A compact recognition card for PowerShell.
patterns.remember: Use this page as a launch point; AI refreshes can expand it into deeper version-aware patterns.

patterns.title: Filter objects instead of parsing text
patterns.code:
Get-Service |
  Where-Object Status -eq "Running" |
  Select-Object Name, DisplayName |
  Sort-Object Name
patterns.why: PowerShell pipelines carry .NET objects, preserving typed properties between commands.
patterns.remember: Use properties with Where-Object/Select-Object; avoid parsing formatted console text.

patterns.title: Turn cmdlet failures into catchable errors
patterns.why: Some cmdlet errors are non-terminating by default; -ErrorAction Stop makes them participate in try/catch.
patterns.remember: Use -ErrorAction Stop when failure must abort the current operation.

patterns.title: Inspect listeners as objects
patterns.code:
Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen |
  Where-Object LocalPort -eq 8000 |
  Select-Object LocalAddress, LocalPort, OwningProcess

Get-Process -Id <OwningProcess>
patterns.why: PowerShell can trace a listening endpoint to its owning process without parsing command-line text.
patterns.remember: connection -> OwningProcess -> Get-Process mirrors the same diagnostic flow as Linux socket tools.

patterns.title: Stream file processing through the pipeline
patterns.why: Pipeline composition lets you enumerate, import and filter many files without manual index loops.
patterns.remember: Let each pipeline stage do one operation on objects.

apis.name: Invoke-RestMethod
apis.whatFor: Call an HTTP API and parse structured results.

practices.title: Service inventory
practices.prompt: List stopped SQL-related services with only useful fields.
practices.reveal: Filter by typed properties and project Name/Status.

practices.title: API automation failure
practices.prompt: A REST call returns an error but the script continues.
practices.reveal: Turn the cmdlet error into a terminating error and handle/rethrow it.

patterns.title: DAX core pattern
patterns.code: CALCULATE, filter context, DIVIDE, REMOVEFILTERS
patterns.why: A compact recognition card for DAX.
patterns.remember: Use this page as a launch point; AI refreshes can expand it into deeper version-aware patterns.

patterns.title: Change filter context with CALCULATE
patterns.code:
Revenue LY =
CALCULATE(
    [Revenue],
    DATEADD('Date'[Date], -1, YEAR)
)
patterns.why: CALCULATE evaluates an expression under modified filter context.
patterns.remember: Ask two questions: what is the current filter context, and what does CALCULATE change?

patterns.title: Build a ratio with a controlled denominator
patterns.code:
Revenue Share =
DIVIDE(
    [Revenue],
    CALCULATE(
        [Revenue],
        REMOVEFILTERS(Product[Category])
    )
)
patterns.why: The denominator removes only the category filter while preserving other report filters.
patterns.remember: Remove exactly the filter you want to ignore; keep the rest of the report context.

patterns.title: Iterate when the expression is row-dependent
patterns.code:
Revenue =
SUMX(
    Sales,
    Sales[Quantity] * Sales[UnitPrice]
)
patterns.why: SUMX evaluates an expression for each row, then aggregates the results.
patterns.remember: Use an iterator when you must calculate per-row logic before aggregation.

patterns.title: Prefer DIVIDE for safe ratios
patterns.code:
Margin % =
DIVIDE(
    [Gross Margin],
    [Revenue]
)
patterns.why: DIVIDE handles zero/blank denominators explicitly and reads like the business calculation.
patterns.remember: For measures, DIVIDE is usually clearer and safer than the / operator.

apis.name: CALCULATE
apis.whatFor: Evaluate a measure under modified filter context.

apis.name: REMOVEFILTERS
apis.whatFor: Clear selected filters inside a context transition.

practices.title: Percent of total
practices.prompt: Category share should ignore category but still respect Date and Region slicers.
practices.reveal: Remove only Product[Category] in the denominator.

practices.title: Row-dependent revenue
practices.prompt: Revenue is Quantity * UnitPrice and no stored revenue column exists.
practices.reveal: Iterate Sales and sum Quantity * UnitPrice per row.

patterns.title: Excel core pattern
patterns.code: XLOOKUP, FILTER, LET, SUMIFS
patterns.why: A compact recognition card for Excel.
patterns.remember: Use this page as a launch point; AI refreshes can expand it into deeper version-aware patterns.

patterns.title: Lookup by a stable key
patterns.code:
=XLOOKUP(
  A2,
  Customers[CustomerID],
  Customers[Segment],
  "Unknown"
)
patterns.why: XLOOKUP separates lookup and return arrays and provides explicit not-found behavior.
patterns.remember: Lookup on stable IDs, not display names.

patterns.title: Name repeated formula expressions with LET
patterns.code:
=LET(
  revenue, B2:B100*C2:C100,
  valid, A2:A100<>"",
  SUM(FILTER(revenue, valid))
)
patterns.why: LET improves readability and prevents repeated evaluation of the same expression.
patterns.remember: Name meaningful intermediate calculations inside long formulas.

patterns.title: Return matching rows as a dynamic array
patterns.code:
=FILTER(
  Orders[[OrderID]:[Amount]],
  Orders[Status]="Open",
  "No open orders"
)
patterns.why: FILTER returns a spilling result set without manual helper columns or copied formulas.
patterns.remember: Think of FILTER as a small declarative WHERE clause over a range/table.

patterns.title: Aggregate with explicit criteria
patterns.code:
=SUMIFS(
  Orders[Amount],
  Orders[CustomerID], A2,
  Orders[Status], "Paid"
)
patterns.why: SUMIFS performs a grouped-style conditional aggregation for a known set of criteria.
patterns.remember: Sum range first, then criteria-range / criteria pairs.

apis.whatFor: Return a matching value by key.

apis.whatFor: Return matching rows as a dynamic array.

practices.prompt: Return segment from CustomerID with a friendly missing fallback.
practices.reveal: Use CustomerID as the lookup key and explicit if_not_found text.

practices.title: Open orders report
practices.prompt: Return only open orders without helper columns.
practices.reveal: Use a Boolean include expression over the table's Status column.

patterns.title: Docker core pattern
patterns.code: multi-stage builds, volumes, service DNS, logs
patterns.why: A compact recognition card for Docker.
patterns.remember: Use this page as a launch point; AI refreshes can expand it into deeper version-aware patterns.

patterns.title: Keep build tooling out of the runtime image
patterns.code:
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM nginx:alpine
COPY --from=build /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html
patterns.why: Multi-stage builds isolate compilers/dependencies from the final runtime image.
patterns.remember: Build in one stage, copy only runtime artifacts into the final stage.

patterns.title: Make service readiness explicit
patterns.code:
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:17
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10
  api:
    build: .
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
patterns.why: Container startup order is not the same as service readiness; health checks make dependencies observable.
patterns.remember: Running does not mean ready. Make readiness a check, then depend on health rather than timing.

patterns.title: Persist mutable state outside the container layer
patterns.code:
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:17
    volumes:
      - db_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data

volumes:
  db_data:
patterns.why: Named volumes survive container recreation and separate durable state from disposable container filesystems.
patterns.remember: Containers are replaceable; durable application state belongs in a volume or external service.

patterns.title: Inspect a running container before rebuilding
patterns.code:
docker ps
docker logs --tail 100 api
docker inspect api
docker exec -it api sh
patterns.why: Logs, metadata and an interactive shell usually reveal runtime failures faster than blindly rebuilding.
patterns.remember: Observe first: logs -> inspect -> exec -> rebuild only when the image really needs to change.

apis.name: docker exec
apis.whatFor: Run a diagnostic command inside a running container.

practices.title: API starts before database is ready
practices.prompt: Compose starts both services but the API fails its first connection.
practices.reveal: Give the database a healthcheck and make the API depend on healthy readiness.

practices.title: Image is unexpectedly huge
practices.prompt: The runtime image contains compilers and package caches.
practices.reveal: Build in one stage and copy only runtime artifacts into the final image.

patterns.title: Git core pattern
patterns.code: status, diff, branch, rebase, reflog
patterns.why: A compact recognition card for Git.
patterns.remember: Use this page as a launch point; AI refreshes can expand it into deeper version-aware patterns.

patterns.title: Build one reviewable commit
patterns.code:
git status
git diff
git add src/feature.ts tests/feature.test.ts
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Add deterministic customer deduplication"
patterns.why: Inspecting before and after staging keeps unrelated changes out of a commit.
patterns.remember: One commit should tell one coherent story that can be reviewed or reverted.

patterns.title: Refresh a private feature branch
patterns.code:
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
# resolve conflicts
git add <resolved-files>
git rebase --continue
patterns.why: Rebasing a private branch replays your work on top of the latest base and can simplify review history.
patterns.remember: Rebase private history; do not rewrite shared history without coordination.

patterns.title: Recover a lost local commit
patterns.code:
git reflog
git show <old-head>
git switch -c recovery <old-head>
patterns.why: Reflog records recent movements of local references even when a commit is no longer reachable from the current branch.
patterns.remember: If you lost a commit after reset/rebase, check reflog before assuming the work is gone.

patterns.title: Park an incomplete working tree safely
patterns.code:
git stash push -u -m "wip: customer import"
git switch hotfix
# ... finish hotfix ...
git switch feature/customer-import
git stash pop
patterns.why: A stash can temporarily clear tracked/untracked work when you must switch context without creating a misleading commit.
patterns.remember: Use stash for short-lived interruption, not as a long-term archive.

apis.name: git restore
apis.whatFor: Restore worktree content or unstage paths.

apis.name: git reflog
apis.whatFor: Inspect local reference movements for recovery.

practices.title: Accidental hard reset
practices.prompt: A local commit disappeared after reset.
practices.reveal: Find the prior HEAD in reflog, inspect it, then create a recovery branch.

practices.title: Hotfix interrupts unfinished work
practices.prompt: You need a clean working tree without committing half-done code.
practices.reveal: Stash tracked/untracked WIP with a message, fix the hotfix, then pop it back.
